findings.issue: The 6-month battery-life requirement is not met by the stated duty cycle and worst-case active current assumptions used by the deterministic check. Firmware wakes every 300 s for 300 ms, and the computed check uses the busiest battery-fed rail peak of 500 mA for that whole wake: 0.3 s / 300 s × 500 mA = 0.5 mA average while awake, plus 9 µA sleep/regulator, for about 0.509 mA total. With a 500 mAh cell, that is about 500/0.509/24 ≈ 41 days, far short of the required 180 days.
findings.suggestion: Provide a realistic active-current average for the wake period and size the power tree/firmware around it, or change the design to a substantially lower-power BLE platform/path. As contracted, the battery-life claim relies on rail average 0.11 mA but does not justify how the ESP32-C3 + BLE advertising + LED blinking fit within that average.

findings.issue: Stored history depth does not plausibly support users checking 'every few days' if longer retrieval is expected. Firmware stores the last 8640 readings, which at 300 s intervals is only 30 days of history, while the brief says users leave it in place and check from their phone every few days; history exists, but the retention horizon is limited relative to the 6-month operating target.
findings.suggestion: If the intended use is to preserve a substantial portion of the 6-month deployment, increase retained records or clarify that only about 30 days of history are available.

findings.issue: The 3.3 V rail falls out of regulation on a 3.5 V Li-ion input according to the power simulation: Vout drops to 3.186 V with -114 mV headroom. A single-cell Li-ion spends much of its discharge below 3.5 V, so this choice works against long runtime and stable operation near the end of battery life.
findings.suggestion: Use a regulator/topology that maintains the required MCU/sensor supply deeper into the cell discharge, or prove the system can meet all requirements over the intended battery voltage range.

items.issue: The 6-month battery-life requirement is not plausibly met as designed. The contract claims 188 days from 0.11 mA average on 3V3, but the firmware is awake 300 ms every 300 s and advertises BLE for 270 ms each cycle. Using the provided duty cycle upper-bound method from the checks: 500 mA peak for 0.3 s every 300 s gives 0.5 mA average, plus 9 µA sleep/LDO ≈ 0.509 mA total, yielding about 500/0.509/24 ≈ 41 days. Even if 500 mA is conservative, the design provides no justified active-current average low enough to support 180 days with BLE advertising every 5 minutes.

The brief says a phone app downloads the stored history, but the contract summary claims approximately 6 months of history while the provided firmware stores only the last 8640 readings, explicitly 30 days at 300 s intervals. With one reading every 5 minutes, 6 months would require roughly 180×24×12 = 51,840 readings, far more than stated.

The 3.3 V rail is out of regulation at 3.5 V battery input in the provided power-path simulation, producing 3.186 V. A single-cell Li-ion spends substantial time below 3.6 V, so this LDO choice works against using most of the 500 mAh cell and therefore against the 6-month runtime target.

findings.issue: The 6-month battery-life requirement is not met by the stated duty cycle and firmware behavior. The rail averages in the contract (0.116 mA total plus 1 µA LDO IQ ≈ 178 days) conflict with the separate duty-cycle-based check and are not substantiated by the active current assumption.
findings.suggestion: Revise the design so the active energy per sample is low enough for 180 days on 500 mAh, or lengthen the sampling interval if allowed. In the contract, provide a power budget consistent with the actual awake current during sensing and BLE advertising, and include the effect of occasional phone connections if they are part of normal use.

findings.issue: Stored history does not meet the product use implied by the brief. The brief says users check every few days and download stored history; the contract summary claims about 6 months of reading history, but the firmware facts say the ring buffer stores only the last 8640 readings, i.e. 30 days at 5-minute intervals. That is a direct inconsistency, and 30 days is not the claimed 6 months.
findings.suggestion: Increase retained history to match the stated requirement/summary, or correct the requirement summary if only 30 days is intended. Ensure firmware partitioning and record format are sized from the actual 4 MB flash so the retained duration is explicit and consistent.

findings.suggestion: Use a regulator/power architecture that maintains a valid 3.3 V rail across the intended Li-ion discharge range, or otherwise justify and constrain the usable battery range so the 6-month requirement remains achievable in practice.

findings.issue: The 6-month battery-life requirement is not met by the stated firmware behavior and power assumptions. The deterministic battery-life check uses the contract/firmware timing: 80 ms awake per 300 s period (30 ms sensor work plus 50 ms BLE advertising) and the busiest battery-fed rail peak of 500 mA, plus 6 µA sleep, yielding about 0.139 mA average and about 150 days from 500 mAh, below the 180-day requirement.
findings.suggestion: Revise the design so the computed average meets 180 days with margin: reduce awake current and/or awake time, reduce the assumed peak rail load if 500 mA is not a realistic wake current, lengthen the reading interval, or use a lower-power BLE platform/regulator path. The contract should also align dutyCycle.activeMs with the actual 80 ms firmware wake.

findings.issue: The contract says USB-C is for charging and flashing firmware, and the ESP32-C3 USB D+/D- mapping supports flashing, but no contract pin or behavior is provided for a USB-controlled reset/boot sequence. With only one exposed button mapped to GPIO9/BOOT, entering the ROM downloader may require a manual button sequence rather than straightforward plug-and-flash use.
findings.suggestion: Make the flashing method explicit in the contract/behavior and ensure it is practical over USB-C without special handling, e.g. document the required manual boot procedure or add circuitry/firmware support for reliable USB flashing.

findings.issue: History storage is only about 30 days at 5-minute intervals, while the brief says users check every few days. This is acceptable for first prototype judging, but longer retention would better fit the product use case.
findings.suggestion: If flash budget allows, increase retained history beyond 30 days or state the intended retention limit more clearly.

payload.text: Brief review of revision 43 (review 3 of at most 3). ## Product brief # Brief: pocket climate logger ## What we want A small battery-powered logger that records temperature and humidity and lets a ph…

findings.issue: The brief requires a status LED that blinks briefly on each reading and shows charging state. The design has two LEDs, but only D1 is connected to firmware as STATUS_LED. The charger LED function is only implied by listing a 'hardware charge LED'; there is no contract behavior for charging indication, and the generated wiring does not include any LED connection to U4.CHRG. As presented, the requirement to show charging state is not plausibly met.
findings.suggestion: Explicitly connect a second LED to the charger status output (for example U4.CHRG through a resistor to the appropriate rail) or otherwise specify and implement charging-state indication in the contract/board wiring.

findings.issue: History retention falls short of the intended use in the contract summary. The firmware stores the last 8640 readings, which is only 30 days at 5-minute intervals. The brief says users check it every few days, so 30 days may be usable, but the summary claims 'target of longer-than-30-day retention at 5-minute intervals if flash budget allows' and this contract does not achieve longer than 30 days.
findings.suggestion: Either relax the summary claim to 30-day retention or increase retained samples/compression so the stored history clearly exceeds 30 days at the specified interval.

findings.issue: Battery-life arithmetic passes on the provided upper-bound check (287 days > 180 days), but the power assumptions are weakly supported because the average is computed using 250 mA peak for the whole 80 ms wake. That gives 0.0727 mA average: 250 mA × 0.08 s / 300 s = 0.0667 mA awake average, plus 0.006 mA sleep/LDO = 0.0727 mA. This still meets 6 months, but the rail averages in the contract (0.051 mA on 3V3 and 0.001 mA on VBAT) are inconsistent with the firmware wake description and are not traceable to actual active currents of the ESP32-C3, BLE advertising, LED blink, and sensor.
findings.suggestion: State a realistic active current budget per part or rail during the 80 ms wake, and align requirements.dutyCycle.activeMs and rail average figures with the actual firmware behavior so the 6-month claim is grounded in the design data.
